newsitem.title: UK: Europe crude outlook - N. Sea oversupply continues.
newsitem.headline: Europe crude outlook - N. Sea oversupply continues.

text.p: The first three Brent cargoes to load in December were clocked on Friday -- an indication of the weak demand for European oil despite a persistent backwardation in the forward market, crude oil traders said.

Although the arbitrage to the United States widened substantially last week, traders said Brent's 48 cent discount to December paper was unlikely to narrow because of a dearth in U.S. demand for December arrival.
Brent would be competing against an oversupplied West African market for the little U.S. demand there was for later dates.
"West African is going to be a bloodbath unless we get a step change in American demand," a Nigerian equity holder said.
Some North Sea traders cited improved refining margins and a widening high/low sulphur fuel oil spread as potential bullish factors for Brent, but the lack of cash buyers unsettled many.
"Brent's not going any lower, but I would not be surprised if it stayed at this level" a North Sea equity holder said.

Some equity holders were optimistic of a slight increase in other North Sea grade premiums, particularly for gas oil-rich Oseberg and Forties. But others argued that larger overall North Sea production in December would work against this.
December-loading Forties was offered at Dated Brent +20 cents on Friday, against the last November loader sold at +15 cents.
"All the programmes are a bit bigger than this month. I can see no reason to go any higher," one trader said.
North Sea crude production from the eight largest fields in December was expected to average just 90,000 barrels per day more than November, according to programmes issued last week.
Sweet domestic U.S. crudes rose versus WTI crude last week, but some recent Brents sailing to the U.S. ended up being sold at a loss, arb dealers said.
"The U.S. just doesn't seem to want any crude arriving in December," a trader said.

The weakness of Brent has been a major impetus behind last week's rise in refining margins, but this could merely serve to stop Brent falling any further, refiners said. A $5 per tonne widening of the high/low sulphur fuel oil spread also favoured sweet crude over sour.
But sour Urals in the Mediterranean was expected to gain 5-10 cents versus Brent next week on supply worries, Mediterranean traders said.
Only two Urals cargoes were still on offer for November.
The largest crude loading berth at Novorossiisk was expected to close for 15 days' maintenance in December, a major Urals buyer said.
